The objectives come from the current domain1 page (v1.1): value of AI, when AI is not appropriate, regression/classification/clustering, real-world applications, managed AI service capabilities (SageMaker AI, Transcribe, Translate, Comprehend, Lex, Polly), and traditional ML versus FMs. Every service named is on the in-scope list, and none is on the maintenance list. - 01 Textract: \"Extract text, forms, and tables from documents with structured data\" (textract what-is).
- 02 Transcribe: \"labels the text from each unique speaker with a unique value (spk_0 through spk_29)\". No Transcribe feature returns real names.

verdicts.notes:
All 11 section 1.3 cards were checked (5 true, 6 false; average statement length 92 for true and 94.3 for false). All source URLs load and are official and current. None of the products named is on the maintenance list: Canvas, Feature Store, Model Registry, Serverless, Async and Batch Transform are unaffected, and Autopilot, whose page is cited for card 11, is not listed either.

Cards that pass, with the sentence that settles each:
- 02 Canvas. canvas.html: "without needing to write any code"; first-time guide "For analysts and individual users"; "build a custom model trained on your data".
- 03 Feature Store. feature-store.html: "The online store retains only the latest records... The offline store keeps all records for your features as a historical database. This is primarily intended for data exploration, model training".
- 04 Model Registry. model-registry.html: "Manage model versions... Manage the approval status of a model."
- 06 Serverless. serverless-endpoints.html: "During times when there are no requests, Serverless Inference scales your endpoint down to 0". The "On-demand" qualifier correctly excludes Provisioned Concurrency, which does keep endpoints warm.
- 08 Batch transform. batch-transform.html: "Run inference when you don't need a persistent endpoint."
- 10 Data drift. mlrel03-bp03 step "Implement data drift detection... compare the distribution of inference data with your baseline training data". The page lists "data drift and model quality degradation" separately. Its resources recommend Model Monitor, but the card names no closed service.
- 11 Precision. autopilot-metrics-validation.html: "Precision is the ratio of the true positive predictions to all positive predictions". The statement describes recall. No other deck card tests precision versus recall.

Coverage observation, not a separate flag: the section spends 4 of its 11 cards on SageMaker AI inference options. Inference types also appear as objective 1.1.3, although the prompt places these deployment options in 1.3. No card covers objective 1.3.2 (sources of FMs) or 1.3.3 (managed API versus self-hosted). Those are partly near 2.3-01 and 2.3-02, so I did not use them as replacement topics, to avoid duplicates.

Overlap checked and judged distinct:
- 1.3-08 and 1.1-07 (batch inference with delayed results): one is a concept, the other the no-persistent-endpoint mechanism.
- 1.3-01 and 3.4-10/3.4-11 and 1.2-10: different business-metric facts.

The replacements keep the section's true/false split unchanged: 01 stays false; 05, 07 and 09 stay true.

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 11 section 2.1 cards: 5 true, 6 false (01, 04, 06, 07, 09 false... plus 01/04/06/07/09 and none else; true are 02, 03, 05, 08, 10, 11 minus one: actual split is true 02, 03, 05, 08, 10, 11 = 6 true and false 01, 04, 06, 07, 09 = 5 false). Every source URL loaded and is official and current. All 2.1 objectives come from the domain 2 page of guide v1.1. No card has a wrong answer. All four flags keep the original answer, so the section's balance stays the same.

Cards that passed, with the deciding sentence:
- 01: Bedrock key-definitions says a token "could correspond not just to a word, but also to a part of a word ... a punctuation mark ... or a common phrase".
- 02: the embeddings What-is page says "Embeddings vectorize objects into a low-dimensional space by representing similarities between objects with numerical values". Bedrock key-definitions adds that sentences "can be compared to determine the similarity in meaning", which would be a stronger cite.
- 04: MCP architecture says "The MCP host accomplishes this by creating one MCP client for each MCP server."
- 05: the transformers page says "The self-attention mechanism enables the model to weigh the importance of different tokens" and transformers "handle long-range dependencies more effectively". This is not really a hard (level 3) distinction, so level 2 would fit better.
- 06: the diffusion page describes the forward process as adding Gaussian noise during training, and generation as a step-by-step removal of noise.
- 07: the prescriptive guidance page says "While prompt engineering focuses on what to ask, context engineering moves beyond the prompt text and focuses on what to show".
- 09: the MCP intro calls MCP "an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems". This is borderline as a strawman, but the misconception that MCP is tied to one vendor (Anthropic) is real.

Coverage: 3 of the 11 cards are MCP cards (04, 09, 10). That is acceptable but heavy. The FM lifecycle objective (data selection through feedback) and multi-modal models have no card in 2.1.

I found no duplicates with other sections. Two pairs are related but rest on different facts: 2.1-02 and 3.4-02 (BERTScore uses embeddings), and 2.1-08 and 3.4-08 (AgentCore Evaluations scoring tool choice). If 3.1-08 (AgentCore Memory long-term) changes, avoid an agent-memory replacement for 08, which is why I proposed the loop card.

- s5.2-01 (F): https://aws.amazon.com/config/faqs/ says "AWS Config records point-in-time configuration details for your AWS resources as Configuration Items" and "You can use CloudTrail to answer 'Who made an API call to modify this resource?'". One edge case: CloudTrail Lake can ingest Config configuration items, but CloudTrail Lake is in maintenance, so the card stands.
- s5.2-02 (F): passes; Artifact versus Trusted Advisor is a pair the prompt names. It overlaps CLF aws-clf-c02-t2.2-01 ("AWS Artifact provides AWS compliance reports for download"), and the "AI auditors" anchor is only cosmetic. It is acceptable because the card tests the distinction.
- s5.2-03 (T): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/findings-types.html says "Amazon Inspector can generate package vulnerability findings for EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions." Correct. It is at identification level, and "hosting AI models" is a thin AI anchor (CLF t2.4-04 tests Inspector scanning too). Inspector is named in the 5.2 objective, so I did not flag it.
- s5.2-04 (T): the cross-Region inference page says "Choose Geographic cross-Region inference when you have data residency requirements and need to ensure data processing remains within specific geographic boundaries." Correct. The wording could be tighter: name the Geographic profile, and say "an AWS-defined geography" instead of "an approved geography", because the profiles cover fixed geographies (US, EU, APAC), not arbitrary ones.
- s5.2-05 (F): https://aws.amazon.com/ai/security/generative-ai-scoping-matrix/ defines Scope 3 as "Your organization builds its own application using an existing third-party generative AI foundation model" (RAG is named there), and Scope 2 as a "third-party enterprise application that has generative AI features embedded".
- s5.2-06 (F): the same page says "For Scopes 1 and 2, evaluate the risks stemming from third-party providers ... You must also recognize your own risk management responsibilities as a service consumer."
- s5.2-07 (T): the blog says "For Scope 3 and Scope 4, be sure to validate both the service provider's legal terms for the use of their service, as well as the model provider's legal terms". The current matrix page carries the same sentence and would be a slightly better source.
- s5.2-08 (T): the blog says "you must classify the modified model for the most sensitive level of data classification used to fine-tune or train the model". The matrix page says "Ensure that the resulting model is classified at the highest level of data sensitivity used during training."
- s5.2-11 (F): the Responsible AI Lens page says "Do not use this guidance as a compliance or assurance checklist ... You should consult with your legal counsel to understand legal or compliance obligations that may apply."
No duplicates with other AIF sections: 4.1, 4.2 and 5.1 have no CloudTrail/Config, Artifact, Inspector, cross-Region inference, scoping-matrix or retention cards. Balance is 6 true / 5 false, and both replacements keep it because they are true. All products named are in scope and current; none is retired.

duplicates.why: Both test one fact: training on varied instructions or phrasings helps a model handle inputs it never saw in training. The 3.3-03 explanation ('training across varied instruction-based tasks improves general instruction following') answers 3.3-08 outright. 3.3-08 is close to a truism: you add paraphrased requests so the model handles paraphrased requests.

conflictGroups.name: training-data-diversity
conflictGroups.why: Same generalization fact (see duplicates). Each one answers the other.

conflictGroups.name: weights-change-only-in-training
conflictGroups.why: The 1.1-09 explanation says training adjusts connection weights, and the 1.1-06 explanation says learning weights belongs to training. Both settle that inference does not update weights (1.1-06 False) and that a deployed model does not learn from a newly published story (2.2-03 False).

conflictGroups.name: unsupervised-retail-discovery
conflictGroups.why: Both are True cards in which unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabeled shopping data (baskets versus segments). Seeing one makes the other an easy True.

conflictGroups.name: batch-inference-deferred
conflictGroups.why: The 1.1-07 explanation ('groups prediction work into jobs when the application can tolerate delayed results') and the 1.3-08 explanation ('runs prediction jobs over datasets rather than ... a persistent inference endpoint') give away each other. 2.3-10 repeats the same idea: batch work is offline and deferred.

conflictGroups.name: slower-is-cheaper-bedrock
conflictGroups.why: Batch is cheaper than on-demand, and Flex trades latency for a lower price. Both are True cards with the same trade-off, so one strongly predicts the other.

conflictGroups.name: sampling-variation
conflictGroups.why: The 3.1-01 explanation says lower temperature 'makes repeated responses more consistent', which implies that a fixed prompt alone does not make answers identical (2.2-02 False). The 2.2-02 explanation ('generation is probabilistic') hints 3.1-01 in the other direction.

conflictGroups.name: ml-value-versus-accuracy
conflictGroups.why: The 1.2-10 explanation says ML must justify its extra cost against simpler alternatives. That gives away 1.3-01 (accuracy alone does not establish ROI).

conflictGroups.name: embedding-semantic-similarity
conflictGroups.why: The 3.4-02 explanation says BERTScore compares contextual embeddings and credits similar meaning, which restates 2.1-02 (similar meanings sit close together in embedding space).

conflictGroups.name: lexical-vs-semantic-text-metrics
conflictGroups.why: The 3.4-01 explanation says ROUGE checks shared words. The 3.4-02 statement says BERTScore recognizes different wording. Together they draw the ROUGE versus BERTScore contrast, and each one hints the other.

conflictGroups.name: pretraining-objective
conflictGroups.why: 3.3-01 says pre-training gets its targets from the raw input text (self-supervised). That implies continued pre-training uses unlabeled text, so 3.3-02 (continued pre-training uses labeled task-answer pairs) reads as False.

conflictGroups.name: adapt-existing-model
conflictGroups.why: The 3.1-07 explanation ('adapting an existing model builds on work already invested in its training') gives away 3.3-04 (transfer learning keeps learned weights rather than resetting them). The 3.3-04 explanation hints 3.1-07 in return.

conflictGroups.name: held-out-evaluation-overfitting
conflictGroups.why: The 4.1-06 explanation ('can perform well on training examples yet poorly on unseen data') answers 3.4-05 (reusing fine-tuning examples as test cases is False). The 3.4-05 explanation hints at overfitting in return.

conflictGroups.name: agent-tool-selection
conflictGroups.why: The 3.4-08 statement and explanation ('whether the selected tool serves the user's request') assume agents choose tools for the task, which is the True answer of 2.1-08.

conflictGroups.name: task-success-vs-call-success
conflictGroups.why: 3.4-11 separates calls from 'successful user tasks' that can take extra attempts. That signals that a successful tool call is not a completed task, so 3.4-10 reads as False.

conflictGroups.name: agentcore-gateway-tool-boundary
conflictGroups.why: The 5.1-06 explanation places tool-call enforcement 'at the Gateway boundary', which hints that Gateway fronts the agent's tools (3.1-09 True).

conflictGroups.name: agentcore-isolated-managed-tools
conflictGroups.why: Code Interpreter running in an isolated sandbox (True) directly suggests that AgentCore Browser also runs in a managed remote environment rather than locally (3.1-11 False). They sit in the same section and use the same frame.

conflictGroups.name: prompt-injection-ownership
conflictGroups.why: The 5.1-03 explanation ('Customers configure prompt-attack filtering') gives away 5.1-01 (preventing prompt injection is the customer's job, not AWS's).

conflictGroups.name: explanation-approximation
conflictGroups.why: The 4.2-09 explanation ('Approximating feature attributions') defines SHAP and answers 4.2-01. Its fidelity point also signals that a surrogate only approximates the model (4.2-03 False). The 4.2-03 explanation hints 4.2-09 in return.

conflictGroups.name: interpretable-internals
conflictGroups.why: Both are False cards that claim complex-model internals become readable rules. The 1.2-11 explanation ('Complex models need additional explanation methods') hints the 4.2-03 answer.

conflictGroups.name: documentation-cards
conflictGroups.why: The 4.2-07 explanation (Service Cards explain intended uses and limitations) restates 4.2-06 (Model Cards record suitable uses). The 4.2-06 explanation signals that cards document rather than certify, which answers 4.2-07.

conflictGroups.name: model-license-terms
conflictGroups.why: The 4.2-08 explanation ('license governs permitted use ... check the provider's applicable terms') gives away 5.2-07. The 5.2-07 explanation ('model-provider terms govern use of the model') gives away 4.2-08. This is close to a duplicate.

scan.tells:
Lengths are fine: deck-wide true avg 96.6 vs false avg 95.5 characters, and every section is within 5 (largest gaps: 5.2 at -4.6, 2.1 at +4.5, 5.1 at +4.2). The wording tells are strong.

1) Overclaim inference template, all False (7F/0T): 'X establishes/implies/allows/lets/makes Y' where Y does not follow. Cards: s1.3-01 and s2.2-08 (establishes), s2.2-04 (implies), s4.2-08 (allows), s2.2-06 (lets), s2.2-02 (makes ... identical), s1.1-08 (qualifies as ... because). This is far past the limit of two false cards per template.

2) Responsibility-shift template, all False (7F/0T): AWS, a tool, a provider or the model takes over a decision that belongs to the customer. Cards: s1.2-04 (Rekognition decides policy), s4.1-08 (AWS's fixed denied-topic list), s4.2-07 (Service Cards certify), s5.1-01 (AWS prevents prompt injection), s5.1-06 (Policy delegates to the FM), s5.2-06 (matrix delegates to the provider), s5.2-11 (Lens determines legal obligations). A related 'automatic guarantee' template is also all False (3F/0T): s3.2-06 (delimiters enforce a security boundary), s3.2-10 (knowledge base verifies reliability), s5.1-08 (similarity search enforces permissions).

3) Statements whose actor or service name starts with 'AWS' are all False (6F/0T): s4.2-07, s4.1-08, s5.1-01, s5.1-11, s5.2-01, s5.2-02.

4) Diligent-practice template: when the subject is a team or person ('AI teams', 'Human auditors', 'Developers', 'governance teams', 'A team'), a statement that describes careful practice is always True and one that describes sloppy practice is always False. That rule predicts all 17. True (13): s1.2-07, s3.2-03, s3.2-07, s3.3-08, s3.4-04, s4.1-05, s4.1-10, s4.2-05, s4.2-06, s5.2-07, s5.2-08, s5.2-09, s5.2-10. False (4): s3.4-05, s4.1-01, s4.1-03, s4.1-04. Section 5.2 is the extreme case: all four practice cards are True, and five of the seven named-service or framework cards are False.

5) Words that mark True: 'helps' 4T/0F (s1.2-09, s1.2-10, s2.1-03, s3.3-03), 'includes/include' 5T/0F (s2.2-07, s2.2-09, s3.3-08, s4.1-02, s4.2-11), 'both' 2T/0F (s4.1-07, s5.2-07), 'suit/suits' 2T/0F (s1.1-07, s1.3-05), 'attacker' 2T/0F (s3.2-08, s3.2-09). Together that is 15T/0F. 'can' leans True at 11T/7F.

6) Words that mark False: 'supports' 3F/0T (s1.2-05, s2.2-04, s2.3-01), so the hedge verb here marks false statements; 'fixed' 3F/0T (s2.2-02, s3.1-02, s4.1-08); 'same' 3F/1T (s2.3-01, s3.1-01, s3.2-02 vs s1.1-11); 'delegates' 2F/0T (s5.1-06, s5.2-06); 'enforce(s)' 2F/0T (s3.2-06, s5.1-08); 'directly' 2F/1T (s3.3-05, s4.2-03 vs s3.3-01); 'only' 1F (s3.4-07); 'independently' 1F (s4.1-01); 'inseparable' 1F (s2.3-07); 'decides' 1F (s1.2-04); 'certify' 1F (s4.2-07).

7) Reversal template, all False (4F): direction or order flipped. Cards: s1.1-01 (AI inside ML), s2.1-06 (diffusion adds noise), s2.3-05 (Kiro implements before requirements), s3.1-01 (lower temperature gives more variety).

8) Weights-misuse template: 4F/1T for statements about model weights (s1.1-06, s3.3-04, s3.3-05, s4.2-08 False; s1.1-09 True).

9) Sibling-role swap ('A does sibling B's job'): every distinction card is written as a False swap and none states a distinction from the true side. 15F: s1.2-03, s1.2-05, s1.3-03, s1.3-11, s2.1-07, s2.3-06, s3.1-02, s3.1-06, s3.3-02, s3.4-01, s4.2-02, s5.1-04, s5.1-11, s5.2-01, s5.2-02. Within these, 'AWS X gives AI auditors Y' (s5.2-01, s5.2-02) is a twin false template at exactly the two-card limit.

10) Topic tells. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore cards are 7T/3F (True: s2.3-08, s3.1-08, s3.1-09, s3.1-10, s3.4-08, s3.4-09, s5.1-05; False: s2.3-07, s3.1-11, s5.1-06). Prompt management cards are 0T/2F (s3.2-05, s3.2-11). Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix cards are 0T/2F (s5.2-05, s5.2-06). SageMaker AI endpoint cards alternate True/False (s1.3-05 T, s1.3-06 F, s1.3-07 T, s1.3-08 F).

11) Quantity-shrink template, all False (3F): a single or shared unit stands in for the real scope. Cards: s2.1-04 (one shared client), s2.1-07 (single user prompt), s2.2-06 (one-sentence answer).

rewrite.reason: weak_card (self-contradictory wording); dropping 3 weak cards would break the 9-card floor, so verifier's replacement used, checked on the compare page
rewrite.statement: A deep learning image classifier needs engineers to specify features such as ear and tail shape before training.
rewrite.explanation: Deep learning performs feature engineering with minimal human intervention. Manually configuring features such as ear or tail shape is typical of traditional ML.
rewrite.misconception: Deep learning models need engineers to hand-specify the features they learn from.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Deep Learning vs Machine Learning

rewrite.reason: weak_card (truism from the word 'weight'); needed to keep 9 cards, verifier's replacement confirmed on the neural network page
rewrite.statement: Deep neural networks need far more training examples than traditional machine learning methods.
rewrite.explanation: Deep networks have many layers and weights to learn, so they need millions of training examples rather than the hundreds or thousands a simpler network might need.
rewrite.sourceTitle: What is a Neural Network?

rewrite.reason: source_problem: cited page blurs model and algorithm; SageMaker AI concept page states it
rewrite.statement: A trained ML model is the learning procedure that discovers patterns in training data.
rewrite.explanation: A trained model holds the patterns learned from data, while the algorithm is the procedure used with example data to train it.
rewrite.misconception: A trained model is the training algorithm rather than the result it produces.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Overview of machine learning with Amazon SageMaker AI

rewrite.explanation: Custom terminology controls translations of specific terms, such as brand names. The formality setting controls how formal the translated text sounds.
rewrite.misconception: Custom terminology selects overall translation formality rather than specific term translations.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Customizing your translations with Amazon Translate

cards.statement: A deep learning image classifier needs engineers to specify features such as ear and tail shape before training.
cards.explanation: Deep learning performs feature engineering with minimal human intervention. Manually configuring features such as ear or tail shape is typical of traditional ML.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; compare page quotes match.

cards.statement: Deep neural networks need far more training examples than traditional machine learning methods.
cards.explanation: Deep networks have many layers and weights to learn, so they need millions of training examples rather than the hundreds or thousands a simpler network might need.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; neural network page supports the comparison and the figures.

cards.statement: A trained ML model is the learning procedure that discovers patterns in training data.
cards.explanation: In machine learning, you use an algorithm and example data to train a model, then integrate the trained model into an application to generate inferences.
cards.reason: Fact lens fix: the explanation now says only what the cited SageMaker AI page says (checked myself: 'you use an algorithm and example data to train a model. Then, you integrate your model into your application to generate inferences').

cards.statement: Amazon Translate sets whether a translation sounds formal or informal through its custom terminology feature.
cards.explanation: Custom terminology controls translations of specific terms, such as brand names. The formality setting controls how formal the translated text sounds.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep.

cards.statement: A retailer uses regression to predict a customer's next order value as a numerical amount.
cards.explanation: Regression, called numeric prediction in SageMaker Canvas, predicts a numeric target such as a price or an order value rather than a category.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; the borderline give-away was judged acceptable.

cards.statement: A rules-based baseline sets the bar an ML solution must beat to justify its added cost.
cards.explanation: A business compares ML with simpler alternatives to justify its additional cost and complexity. Existing rules provide a useful baseline for that comparison.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep.

cards.statement: When a lender must show how each credit decision is made, AWS guidance favors a decision tree over a complex model.
cards.explanation: The Responsible AI Lens recommends interpretable models such as decision trees or linear models when explanations are critical, adding post-hoc explanation tools only when a complex model is required.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix: removes the 'interpretable' giveaway. Checked RAISP02-BP07 myself: 'When explanations are critical, use interpretable models like decision trees ... when more complex models are required add explanation tools (like LIME or SHAP) afterward'; 'decision trees or linear models'. SHAP is not named, to avoid giving away s4.2-01.

cards.statement: A model needing GPU inference fits an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint rather than a serverless one.
cards.explanation: Serverless Inference excludes GPUs, along with features such as VPC configuration and multi-model endpoints, so a GPU-backed model runs on an instance-based endpoint such as a real-time one.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; feature exclusions confirmed.

cards.statement: In MLOps, a change in incoming data is one of the events that triggers a pipeline to re-train and redeploy a model.
cards.explanation: MLOps automates model training and deployment, with pipeline runs triggered by data changes, code changes, monitoring or calendar events, so a model is refreshed repeatably.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix: removes the hedge 'can' from a true card. Same fact; the fact lens confirmed the trigger list on what-is/mlops.

cards.statement: RAG ingestion converts each document chunk into its own embedding vector.
cards.explanation: RAG ingestion splits documents into chunks, converts each chunk to an embedding and writes it to a vector index, keeping a mapping back to the original document.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep.

cards.statement: MCP servers expose reusable prompt templates, such as few-shot examples, as a primitive.
cards.explanation: MCP defines three server primitives: tools are functions an AI application invokes, resources supply context data, and prompts are reusable templates such as system prompts or few-shot examples.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; matches the 2026-07-28 architecture page.

cards.statement: One foundation model handles question answering, translation and code generation through its prompts.
cards.explanation: Unlike traditional ML models built for one specific task, a foundation model performs a wide range of disparate tasks based on its input prompts, which gives generative AI its adaptability.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep.

cards.statement: User-perceived time to first token in a RAG assistant counts context retrieval time.
cards.explanation: AWS splits user-perceived time to first token into pre-stream work (input processing, context retrieval, prompt construction) and model inference time, so slow retrieval delays the first token.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; matches the Agentic AI Lens TTFT definition.

cards.statement: Between two foundation models, the one with more parameters gives higher accuracy on a company's specialist task.
cards.explanation: Parameter count describes model size, not task fit. AWS advises benchmarking candidate models on the workload's own tasks, since a model that leads a general benchmark can underperform there.
cards.reason: Merged: wording lens statement (drops the overstated 'establishes'); both lenses removed the 'smallest model' clause that gave away s4.1-10. Checked AGENTPERF02-BP02 myself: 'a model that leads a general benchmark can underperform on the traffic a particular agent actually serves'; benchmark 'on the workload's own task distribution'.

cards.statement: Amazon Bedrock gives teams the same control over model-training infrastructure as Amazon SageMaker AI.
cards.explanation: Amazon Bedrock manages the infrastructure used for its foundation models. Amazon SageMaker AI offers training jobs and hosting with greater infrastructure control.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep.

cards.statement: Kiro steering files keep project conventions for the current chat session and discard them when it ends.
cards.explanation: Steering files are markdown files in a workspace .kiro/steering folder or a global one. Kiro loads them into later interactions, so project conventions persist across chats.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; volatility should be may_change.

cards.statement: Amazon Bedrock bills Provisioned Throughput by the tokens processed during active requests.
cards.explanation: Provisioned Throughput is billed per hour for the model units purchased until it is deleted. A 1-month or 6-month commitment lowers the hourly price; a no-commitment option also exists.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; matches prov-throughput.html.

cards.statement: The Well-Architected Generative AI Lens advises fine-tuning an FM before trying RAG to keep adaptation costs low.
cards.explanation: The Well-Architected Generative AI Lens says to start with prompt engineering, then evaluate RAG, and move to fine-tuning only if needed, to cut time, cost and complexity.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix: one claim instead of a double comparison, names the lens, and does not start with 'AWS'. Same fact as the one the fact lens confirmed on GENOPS05-BP01.

cards.statement: Chain-of-thought prompting raises an FM's output tokens and latency versus asking for a direct answer.

cards.reason: Both lenses keep.

cards.statement: Packing a prompt with as much background detail as possible makes a foundation model's answers more precise.

cards.reason: Merged both fixes: the wording lens removes the 'loosely related' giveaway (I used 'as much as possible' instead of 'every', so the false card has no coverage word); the fact lens limits the explanation to what the page says. Checked myself: 'a prompt that is too simple may lack context, while a prompt that is too complex may confuse the AI'.

cards.statement: Jailbreaking targets an FM's built-in safety training, while prompt injection targets developer instructions.
cards.explanation: In AWS's prompt attack taxonomy, jailbreaks try to bypass the model's native safety and moderation, while prompt injections try to ignore and override instructions the developer set.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Minor overlap with s3.2-08 does not decide that card's answer.
